# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.

# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in [competition deals](competition-deals.md).

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterfinal | 4 | 16 | 8 |
| Semifinal | 6 | 36 | 18 |
| Final | 8 | 64 | 32 |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md). The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

[Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md), [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) and [card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [layout grid](../visuals/layout-grid.md) and [zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md).

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md) covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md) explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.

[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.

# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.

Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.

The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.

## Laptop: learning the faces aloud

In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”

Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.

This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.

The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.

## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation

Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.

This was a useful correction to the observation method. Card navigation and memory retrieval are separate activities, even when they occur between the same two reveals. Counting only the delay between clicks would have concealed the difference entirely, since this participant was not primarily clicking.

Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.

The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.

## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own

In the tablet session, moving the device between people interrupted the group's visual reference. The outgoing player tilted it toward the next person, while another participant tried to read the result from an angle. The result was still present, but not everyone saw it at the same time.

The next player first adjusted the tablet on the table, then looked for the board. That sequence would have been easy to describe as slow play if the observer had measured from physical handoff. It was mostly positioning the device. The observation helped separate the social transition from actual interaction with the game.

People also used the visible completed board as a conversation piece. They pointed at remembered mistakes and explained how they finally located a pair. The exposed cards carried a short history of the attempt that a bare result number would not capture. In a group setting, that retrospective conversation was part of the appeal.

The presentation of a competition handoff remained undecided. The prototype used ordinary play and a paper event sketch. It showed what people looked at and discussed. [Competition overview](competition-overview.md) explains the intended social context.

## Phone: scrolling and tapping had different purposes

On the phone, Niko sometimes touched the board to move its visible area rather than to reveal a card. His comments made that intention clear: he was searching for a remembered row near the edge. A raw touch trace would have contained contact with several cards, but contact alone would not have described the intended action.

The research note therefore distinguishes an attempted tap, a completed activation and a scroll gesture. These are useful observational categories, not additional game states. A participant saying “I touched that one” can refer to any of them, and the distinction can explain an apparent missing move.

The observer's view was narrower on the phone too. People beside the player often saw the device's back or an oblique angle, so they talked more about the eventual result than about individual reveals. That was a different social experience from the laptop, even though the underlying card actions were unchanged. [Pointer and touch](../interface/pointer-and-touch.md) and [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md) cover the relevant existing behavior.

## The mismatch pause helped memory and confused tapping

Several exchanges centered on a miss. One participant used the visible interval to repeat both face descriptions aloud. Another tapped quickly again and interpreted the lack of a new reveal as a lost input. The two reactions came from different expectations about whether the turn had finished.

It was useful in the discussion to replay the participant's explanation in ordinary language: “I was still looking at those two” versus “I thought I could choose the next one.” Both describe a reading of the same moment. Neither requires a different deck or a new scoring mechanism to explain it.

## Spectators remembered more than the current player expected

People who watched closely often remembered a location that the player had forgotten. Sometimes that produced a laugh; sometimes it produced an unsolicited hint. When the device moved out of view, conversation changed from specific positions to general encouragement. The physical setting strongly influenced how much information was shared.

This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.

A future research session could explore how different groups feel about spectating, but that is a research question rather than a committed feature. The existing observations support only the narrower conclusion that sharing a device also shares attention in ways that vary with posture, distance and familiarity.

## Evidence retained from the discussion

These sessions identified misunderstandings during local play. Shape-only memory, keyboard travel, device adjustment and the visible mismatch interval each explain a different kind of report. The observations are useful starting points for further sessions.

A board code can anchor an arrangement, a snapshot can anchor progress and a replay can anchor actions. The observer's account adds the human context those artifacts omit. [Competition deals](competition-deals.md), [browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) and [acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) explain the technical evidence.
# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. [Status bar](../interface/status-bar.md) explains the existing statistics, and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains the surrounding composition.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [new game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) describe the existing interactions.

# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.
# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.
# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity.
