# ADR 040: Keep the delivered game compact

This record explains the compact-artifact aim and its architectural tradeoffs.

## Context

The one-file distribution should be easy to retain and pass along. Generated artwork, a system font and a narrow runtime help keep that artifact manageable. The team wanted compact delivery, with no maximum HTML byte count specified.

The size rules that are explicit concern authored TypeScript files: an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 lines per file. Those limits are about reviewable behavior modules, not compressed distribution size. Conflating the two would make a smaller source file look like proof of a smaller bundle when it might simply add another import.

## What actually affects the artifact

React and React DOM are bundled runtime dependencies. Vite and its plugins transform the source during the build. The face renderer describes shapes with a small set of SVG primitives rather than embedding 128 raster images. The system font avoids a downloaded or inlined font asset. There is no audio collection to carry with the file.

A single inline file also has no chunk-preload purpose. The main configuration disables the helper and the output test checks its absence. That removes irrelevant runtime machinery, though the reason is the offline contract rather than a claim about a particular number of saved bytes. [ADR 003](adr-003-single-file.md) explains delivery.

## Source structure is a separate optimization

Small modules make changes easier to review and focused tests easier to locate. They do not require collapsing every abstraction to reduce import statements. The build combines source modules into the final artifact, so a clear behavior boundary can remain in source without becoming another file the player must copy.

The current source audit measures authored TypeScript line counts and checks several source conventions. It does not report a universal bundle-size threshold. A developer reading this record can distinguish an enforced source constraint from a qualitative artifact aim. [Source audit notes](../architecture/source-audit-notes.md) and [ADR 057](adr-057-small-components.md) explain that evidence.

## Alternatives

Removing React could reduce runtime code, but would exchange framework bytes for custom rendering and lifecycle work. Replacing generated SVG with raster sprites might compress differently, but would create asset maintenance and minimum-size review costs. Splitting the output into cached files could benefit a repeatedly visited hosted site while weakening the copy-one-file distribution path.

The project accepted the runtime framework in exchange for clear state-driven rendering. It rejected unnecessary remote assets and diagnostic code in the shipped entry. These are explicit architectural trades, not an assertion that the current bundle is the smallest possible implementation of a memory game.

## Measurement and interpretation

A meaningful artifact comparison uses the same build tools and compares the produced `dist/index.html`. Source character count, compressed transfer size and disk size answer different questions.

Diagnostic face-sheet and session outputs are separate builds. Their size should not be confused with the game artifact, just as test-result screenshots should not be counted as shipped resources. [ADR 051](adr-051-test-artifacts.md) explains that separation.

The practical aim is to keep additions proportionate to a bounded offline game while preserving readable code and correct input. [Dependency policy](../architecture/dependency-policy.md), [Build pipeline](../architecture/build-pipeline.md) and [ADR 029](adr-029-pinned-versions.md) provide the neighboring context. The existing requirements and tests define what must pass today.

## The authored-source size check

The implemented size check counts lines in authored TypeScript. It should not be reported as a measurement of the final HTML bundle.

```ts
test('authored TypeScript stays small, uses static ESM and rejects unsafe type escapes', async () => {
  const files = (await Promise.all(['src', 'scripts', 'tests', 'art'].map(sourceFiles))).flat();
  for (const file of files.filter((file) => /\.tsx?$/.test(file.path))) {
    assert.ok(file.text.trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/).length <= 200, file.path);
    assert.doesNotMatch(file.text, /@ts-(?:ignore|nocheck|expect-error)/);
    assert.doesNotMatch(
      file.text,
      /\bany\b|\bas\s+(?:[A-Z{]|unknown\b|number\b|string\b)|\bimport\s*\(|\brequire\s*\(/,
    );
  }
});
```
# Performance budget
This page describes the performance constraints already present in Neon Pairs and how to investigate first render and input work.

There is no numeric first-render, input-latency, frame-rate, bundle-byte or memory budget in the specification or test configuration. The current enforceable constraints are functional: the distribution is self-contained, every supported board renders, input remains usable in the specified layouts, and game time follows active elapsed time rather than callback frequency. Browser-test timeouts are automation allowances.

## What the current numbers mean

Several timing values occur in the source, but each has a specific job:

| Value | Owner | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 40ms | `session/browser-clock.ts` | Ordinary scheduling interval for active clock updates |
| 800ms | `game.ts` | Active duration of a mismatching pair |
| 120ms | `board/card.css` | Border-color transition duration |
| 600ms | `status/status.css` | Single completion pulse duration |
| 15000ms | `tests/browser-test.ts` | Default browser assertion allowance |
| 30000ms | `tests/browser-test.ts` | Standard case timeout |
| 90000ms | `tests/browser-test.ts` | Longer case timeout for larger journeys |

The first four values describe game scheduling or presentation. The last three allow an automated verifier to complete on a busy machine. A test finishing in twenty seconds does not establish that a card responds within twenty seconds, and a 40ms clock update interval is not a promise about input latency.

Likewise, the caps on elapsed time and moves are data limits. They prevent unbounded counters and preserve valid formats. The snapshot and replay byte limits constrain accepted input, not the size of the shipped HTML. [Elapsed-time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) and [Data exchange](../sharing/data-exchange-policy.md) describe those separate contracts.

## First render: what is actually loaded

The production entry is `index.html`, which loads `src/main.tsx`. Vite builds it with React integration and `vite-plugin-singlefile`. `vite.config.ts` targets ES2023 and disables the module-preload helper. The emitted `dist/index.html` carries the game script, styles and inline artwork.

This removes external request dependencies from the play path. It does not remove JavaScript parse, React initialization, storage access, deck generation, DOM construction, style calculation or paint. A single file can still be expensive to initialize, so request count alone is incomplete evidence for first render.

The offline journey in `play.e2e.test.ts` opens the disk URL with the browser context offline. It expects the default 16-card board and a successful reveal, while the observed request list contains only the document navigation. `build-output.e2e.test.ts` separately checks the HTML for the `fetch(` and `relList` markers. These are delivery checks; neither records a first-paint timestamp.

The main build and diagnostic builds have different contents. `.art/index.html` renders all 128 face identities at once. `.session/index.html` includes the cleanup harness. Measuring either diagnostic page as the game startup cost would misrepresent the artifact users receive. The game distribution does not include those entry controls.

## Initial board size changes the workload

The default is a 4x4 board unless valid saved preferences select another supported size. A fresh HTTP context with no preferences and a warm context remembering 16x16 therefore have different first-render workloads. A report that omits storage state can compare unlike runs.

The largest board has 256 card buttons. All are rendered even if the board viewport shows only part of them. The layout uses internal scrolling to preserve card geometry; it does not virtualize rows or create cards lazily as the player scrolls.

Hidden cards mount the neutral back, not their face SVG. `Board.tsx` passes `null` for a hidden face and `Card.tsx` chooses the back markup. This serves the hidden-information contract and reduces initial artwork. Revealed and matched cards mount their SVGs, so a completed large board has a different rendering cost from the same board before any reveal.

The deck is generated from the code before it can be rendered. Generation is small and bounded by the supported sizes, but the documentation contains no measured duration for it. The independent generator checks establish correct ordering, not execution speed. Replacing generation for speed still has to preserve the version 1 deal.

## Input: follow the work rather than the click count

The card's native click handler calls the shared activation function and then performs nearest scrolling for the clicked element. `use-game.ts` synchronizes the active clock before applying `activateSession`. The pure action validates the index and current selection, then returns an unchanged or updated state.

That synchronous clock sampling is essential when a scheduled callback is late. An overdue mismatch must resolve before the next valid reveal is considered. Removing synchronization to shorten an input handler could make a trace look cheaper while reintroducing a lost-click defect. The fractional-clock browser case protects this ordering.

Keyboard arrows use a different path. `navigationTarget` computes a destination; the focus hook focuses it with browser scrolling suppressed and applies nearest alignment when appropriate. Focus movement does not reveal cards or add moves. A performance investigation can therefore distinguish an arrow-navigation cost from a reveal cost without changing the product behavior.

The clipped-pointer tests cover a particularly sensitive arrangement. Moving a card during the press can lose the release. The implementation waits for a completed click before pointer-related nearest scrolling. A change that eagerly scrolls on all focus events could reduce a later layout step but break activation at the board edge. [Regression catalogue](regression-catalogue.md) describes that failure.

## Work avoided on clock-only renders

`Board.tsx` memoizes the visible-position set from `matched` and `selection`, and the matched-position set from `matched`. A clock tick that changes neither input can reuse them. This avoids rebuilding the lookup collections solely because elapsed time changed.

`Card` is wrapped with React's `memo`. The board keeps a stable activation callback that invokes the latest handler through a ref. Focus and navigation callbacks come from the board focus hook. When a tick changes no card props, memoized cards can skip rendering even though the surrounding game and status update.

While a mismatch is pending, `advanceGame` creates a new selection with reduced remaining time. The set memo then has a changed dependency, although the two visible positions may be the same. Card props can still compare equal because they receive face, match and tab-stop values rather than the entire selection object.

A focus change updates tab indices for the remembered old and new card. A reveal changes the face prop of the newly exposed position. A match changes the two relevant matched flags. The parent maps the bounded deck, while memoization narrows child rendering. There is no global state library, worker-based board renderer or canvas layer in this implementation.

## Scheduling correctness under load

The session hook uses `performance.now` observations to calculate active deltas. The timeout is a request to sample again, not the source of elapsed truth. When a callback is delayed, the next sample accounts for elapsed active time instead of adding one fixed tick.

When a mismatch has less than an ordinary interval remaining, the scheduled delay is the smaller value. Visibility changes synchronize against the prior visible state, update visibility and reschedule. Imported pause and completion affect whether the clock is running. Cleanup clears work and removes the listener.

This design tolerates delayed presentation while preserving game data. It does not promise a particular paint cadence during host contention. The controlled-clock suite proves arithmetic and ordering, while a real browser trace is needed to diagnose long tasks or stuttering on a particular device. [Flaky-test notes](flaky-test-notes.md) separates those two investigations.

## Collecting a useful measurement

A first-render investigation can use the existing distribution and browser performance tools without adding product telemetry. Keep the artifact, actual browser version, origin, viewport and saved-size state with the observation. A clean default board and a context remembering 16x16 have different workloads; cold and warm loading also answer different questions.

Inspect navigation through the first usable controls and board. The trace can distinguish script evaluation, React initialization, synchronous preference access, layout and paint. An absent network waterfall or a screenshot after navigation supplies no startup duration by itself.

For input, compare first reveal, matching and mismatching second reveals, large-board navigation and session replacement. A completed 16x16 board has more SVG content than a hidden one. Keep actual coordinate presses for hit-testing complaints; a direct DOM click isolates event ordering but bypasses that geometry.

The source contains no measured median or tail timings for these paths. A before/after report needs comparable conditions before attributing a difference to code. The current structural choices explain costs without establishing a numerical latency claim.

## Release interpretation

The release process checks the complete supported workloads and offline delivery, then records the runtime actually used. No existing test enforces a millisecond first-render threshold or a byte ceiling for the HTML. A release report can therefore state that the functional checks passed on the recorded combination, while leaving measured responsiveness unspecified.

If an investigation finds a visible slowdown, preserve the reproduction and trace with its conditions, then use the relevant unit and browser regressions to verify the repair. [Known issues](known-issues.md) records the current measurement gap, and [Release checklist](release-checklist.md) keeps build correctness, compatibility and manual acceptance separate from performance claims.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.
# Sound
Sound is a game requirement that keeps Neon Pairs silent.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can play in a shared room without starting audio. Card feedback and completion are conveyed by the game display and accessible announcements.

## Playback

- S01 - Keep the game silent for every action and state, including a reveal, a match, a mismatch, a restart and a win.

- S02 - Include no audio files, audio API calls or sound toggle in this version. Silence is the required behavior, not an unfinished feature.

## Feedback

The game communicates card states and completion through its [visual design](../visuals/visuals.md). Turn results also use the [input announcements](../interface/input.md#announcements), so playing doesn't depend on hearing an event.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
